source.title: Theory of Optimal Learning Rate Schedules and Scaling Laws for a Random Feature Model

record.file_problem: None; the full paper, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It derives and evaluates loss-scaling and compute-allocation results in a power-law random-feature model, a different method and setting from the original language-model scaling studies.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports ResNet and GPT-style transformer learning-rate transfer experiments, but those results concern how optimal base learning rates change with training horizon, not the loss-power-law or compute-optimal-allocation outcomes in the claim versions. The paper's cited scaling-law results are not recorded as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: Not a language-model scaling study. The paper derives and numerically checks loss-scaling exponents in a linear power-law random-feature model trained with SGD. Within that model it shows the loss exponent with training horizon depends on the LR, batch and momentum schedule and on the task spectrum (a, b), and that the compute-optimal N/data split depends on (a, b). This is a specific theoretical argument bearing on V7 (schedule- and setup-dependence of exponents and split). It bears more weakly on V3: the allocation is a power of compute, but only in a toy model. Its GPT-2 and ResNet experiments study learning-rate transfer, not loss power laws.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that in a power-law random-feature model the optimal SGD learning-rate schedule is polynomial decay in the easy phase (a > b) and WSD-like in the hard phase (b > a). These schedules beat optimal constant and power-law schedules in scaling exponent, reaching (a-1)/max(a,b). Batch ramps cut wall-clock time in the easy phase, and optimal momentum improves the hard-phase exponent. The authors read ResNet/CIFAR-5M as hard-phase behaviour and GPT-2/C4 as easy-phase behaviour for LR transfer. The compute-optimal allocation is a side result in Appendix B.2.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an analytically tractable power-law random-feature model, optimal-control analysis, and learning-rate schedule experiments rather than the original language-model loss-scaling procedures. It also derives schedules and allocations, rather than reproducing the original scaling-law measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss-scaling exponents and optimal schedules depend on the feature/task exponents a and b, including whether the setting is in the easy or hard phase; the reported loss exponent also varies with learning-rate and batch-schedule choice.

fits_no_version.finding: In GPT-2-style 125M models on C4 (1B–16B tokens, Adam), the optimal base LR decreases with token horizon even under cosine annealing. In ResNets on CIFAR-5M, the optimal base LR is roughly constant under annealing. Short-anneal WSD schedules beat full polynomial annealing for ResNets (Fig. 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal learning rates and schedules transfer across training horizon depending on task spectral structure (easy vs hard phase).

fits_no_version.finding: In the hard phase, jointly optimizing momentum and learning-rate schedules improves the loss-scaling exponent beyond SGD's (a-1)/b (Fig. 3d–f). The improved exponent is not derived analytically.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice (momentum schedules) changes loss-scaling exponents in the random-feature model.

record.problems: The compute-allocation results are derived for a theoretical random-feature model under stated assumptions, not established across language models. The paper says its theory is focused on linear models trained with SGD and does not capture more sophisticated optimizers; it also notes that the improved hard-phase momentum exponent has not been derived analytically. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the catalogued scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: The ResNet CIFAR-5M and GPT-style C4 experiments on learning-rate transfer and annealing are not included because their reported outcomes do not measure the loss-power-law or compute-optimal-allocation versions. Figure-only values for those experiments were not extracted.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss power law in N, D or C. The GPT-2 runs are a single 125M model with LR sweeps.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Allocation in actual language models; no comparison with Kaplan or Hoffmann numbers.
Not tested as a power-law form in other modalities. The ResNet CIFAR-5M runs measure LR transfer only.
Not tested in language models. Parameter counting, data choice, fitting method and curve bending are not tested; the dependence is shown only on schedule and task spectrum in a linear model.

missing.what: Numerical fitted exponents verifying the theory: constant 0.36, power law 0.36, optimal 0.52 (hard); constant 0.56, power law 0.58, optimal 0.69 (easy).
Momentum schedule improves the hard-phase exponent over SGD, shown as fitted exponents across a/b.
Batch-ramp fits at fixed Btot: 0.70 (optimal η), 0.73 (ramp), 0.55 (constant); 33× fewer steps.

record.verdict_notes: All catalogued results come from a linear toy model. Researchers should weigh them as a theoretical argument for schedule- and spectrum-dependence of exponents (V7), not as evidence about language models. In this model Hoffmann's equal split cannot arise, since the data exponent a/(a+1) > 1/2 for a > 1. The paper does not discuss this point. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: The random-feature analysis reports test-loss scaling with training horizon, and the deep-network experiments compare learning-rate schedules. It does not test held-out pretraining loss power laws in language models as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No test of fitting power laws on small runs and predicting much larger runs is reported.

The compute-optimal allocation is derived for the paper's random-feature model under its stated assumptions; it does not compare the original language-model parameter/token allocation results or test a broad range of language models.
The paper does not vary depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
It does not test other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer as instances of the same power-law form.
No downstream-task performance scaling or prediction from pretraining loss is tested.

The results show dependence on task spectral exponents and schedule choice, but do not test parameter-counting conventions, alternative fitting methods, data choices in the original language-model studies, or systematic departure from small-run fits.

relationships.condition: Linear power-law random-feature model with SGD, easy and hard phases (theory plus numerical optimal control)
relationships.reason: The loss exponent with T changes with schedule: constant or power-law LR gives (a-1)/(a+b-1), while the optimal schedule gives (a-1)/max(a,b), with Fig. 2 fits of 0.36 vs 0.52 and 0.56 vs 0.69 (r1–r3, r5–r7). The compute-optimal split depends on task exponents (r9, r10).
relationships.display_finding: The loss exponent with training time changed from (a−1)/(a+b−1) under constant or power-law learning rates to (a−1)/max(a,b) under optimal scheduling, with fitted comparisons of 0.36 versus 0.52 and 0.56 versus 0.69, while compute-optimal allocation depended on task exponents.

tranche.reason: The analytical random-feature model and numerical optimal-control experiments address the scaling question through a different method. Their schedule-dependent exponents support V7 and their power-law allocations support V3; they do not establish that either version is wrong or needs restating.
